facts.text: Frontenac got its name in 1859, honoring French governor Louis de Buade de Frontenac, echoing the area's 18th‑century French exploration at Fort Beauharnois.
In 1857, the Garrard brothers and Westervelt bought over 4,000 acres from Jane Wells and Elizabeth Faribault, using half‑breed scrip to plat the townsite.
Old Frontenac still has an 1868 Christ Episcopal church, unpaved streets, no streetlights, and a dark‑sky aesthetic that harks back to its roots.
Frontenac’s economy moved from fur trading and limestone quarrying to a late‑19th‑century resort for wealthy East Coast and European visitors.
When the Paul and Pacific Railroad built a line near Frontenac in the 1870s, the town’s founders refused to sell land, so the tracks ran a mile away.
In 1974, the Florence Township Heritage Preservation Commission formed to protect Frontenac’s rural character and historic integrity from erosion and groundwater threats.
